title: Anti-Sicilians For Black
description: A supplementary course to learning the Sicilian Defense. Learn to beat the Alapin, Smith-Morra, Rossolimo, and more.

r1b1k2r/ppq1bppp/2n2n2/1BppN3/8/8/PPPP1P.text:
The simple ...Qc7 defends the position and we are ready to castle.

We have all the freedom in the world and White is never better here.

r1bqk2r/p2pbppp/2p3n1/2p1p3/N3P3/3PBN2/P.text: White does not have a useful way to create meaningful threats.

r1bqk2r/p3bppp/2pp2n1/2p1p3/N3P3/3PBN2/P.text:
We will play ...0-0, ...Rb8, and we can even play for a potential ...f5 pawn break.

Like I said, a more challenging way to play is for White to find the maneuver Ne2 to g3 and to f5, but we will play for ...f5 ourselves, challenging this plan.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/1BppN3/8/8/PPPP1PP.text:
White centralizes the knight, attacking our pinned piece.

But nothing to worry about.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p1p1n1/2p5/4P3/2NP1N2/.text:
Standard development from White.

...e5 was our plan all along. 

We want moves like ...Be7 and ...d6 to open up our other bishop. White has lost all their opening advantage.

Natural moves for White include: 8.Be3, 8.h3 and 8.Re1. White also has the maneuver Ne2, Ng3, and Nf5 if they're able to find it.

r1bqkb1r/p2p1ppp/2p3n1/2p1p3/4P3/2NPBN2/.text:
For instance, 8.Be3 is a popular way to continue development.

We will castle kingside.

r1bqkb1r/p2p2pp/2p1pn2/2p1N3/8/8/PPPP1PP.text:
And we'll simply continue development with the knight coming to f6 and the bishop coming to e7 or d6 soon.

We can play ...d6 even though our c6-pawn would be hanging.

If White were to take it, their knight would get trapped.

r1bqkb1r/p2pnppp/2p1p3/2p5/4P3/3P1N2/PPP.text:
White advances with d3, which is safer than d4 and continues to neutralize our light-squared bishop, which might have wanted to develop to a6.

We don't want to face any Bg5 complications, so we'll bring the knight to g6 right away.

We'll be playing on the dark squares and support this with the queen on c7 if needed.

Our bishop will develop to e7 and we'll castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
White can give a check and improve with tempo, which is a benefit of developing the kingside early.

We will block with the bishop, naturally.

r1bqkbnr/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2p1P3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
An interesting move to consider is 5.e5, played 7% of the time.

It might seem like White has seen through our plans and wants to shut down our expansion immediately.

We won't let it happen. Challenging the structure is a good antidote.

White shouldn't play d4 because of ...Ba6 ideas and capturing on f6 would only improve our development.

r1bqkbnr/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Going for d4 at this point is an inaccuracy, even though it happens more than 15% of the time.

White shouldn't really mix the d4-approach and the Rossolimo.

We've got a strong response which is ...Ba6.

It makes sense if you think about it: White has traded off their light-squared bishop and opened up the diagonal after d4.

Now it's going to be hard for them to castle.

r1bqkbnr/p2p1ppp/2p1p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White castles.

You will face this move 40% of the time.

Good supporting moves for our idea are ...Qc7, or ...Ne7 to ...Ng6.

5.Nc3 and 5.d3 most often transpose to this main line.

As it's more natural to develop the minor pieces first we will bring our knight out.

r1bqkbnr/p2p2pp/2p1pp2/2p1P3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
Instead, White castles.

This allows us to take in the center.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2B1p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
This study will deal with White capturing on c6 right away, which happens almost half the time.

Recapturing towards the center is more natural.

Our plan is to play on the dark squares with ...d6 and ...e5.

It might seem more natural to go for the ...d5 expansion, but our bishop on c8 would remain blocked in.

By playing on the dark squares, we'll make sure to develop it.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2p5/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
White castles.

They've given us central space, so why not make use of it?

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
The Rossolimo is characterized by 3.Bb5.

It's played 12% of the time.

White develops the bishop to b5 instead of c4, where it's less of a target, and pressures our knight on c6.

In terms of potentially removing our one piece controlling the center, this move makes sense.

I recommend ...e6 as a defensive measure. 

If White doesn't capture immediately, our knight is coming to e7 to support the knight on c6.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
The second most popular move at amateur level is 3.Bc4, played 18% of the time.

At this stage, that is still almost 24 million games in the database!

White wants to develop the kingside knight and bishop first, to the most "traditional" squares, in Italian style.

We'll play ...e6 right away, aiming for ...d5. It will come with tempo on the bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2pP4/2B5/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White captures.

But we maintain two pawns in the center.

White will have to move the bishop again.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1Bpp4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
They will probably slide it to b5 now, but one can make an argument that it was better to play Bb5 from the get-go.

White doesn't have serious pressure and has allowed us essential central expansion.

We can just continue developing.

r2qk1nr/p2p1ppp/b1p1p3/2b5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White develops the knight to c3.

The light-squared bishop has been activated so our plans in the center change.

r2qk1nr/p4ppp/b1p1p3/2bp4/4P3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Now we want to expand with ...d5!

We've got all one wants in the opening.

Central space and monster pieces.

Next, we'll finish kingside development and castle.

r2qkbnr/p2p1ppp/b1p1p3/2P5/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Taking on c5 makes matters even worse for them.

We'll recapture and keep a strong bishop pair.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight behind the pawn.

This is the most popular main line move.

We'll activate our knight as well, further controlling the d4-square.

This is an alternative to 2...d6.

From here on, d4 is the most common move, but White has some other options.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our course on Anti-Sicilians for Black!

In the first study of Chapter 1, we'll take a look at White playing 3.Bc4 and some variations in the Rossolimo, 3.Bb5.

3.Bc4 could be considered dubious as it gives us easy development and central space.

On the other hand, 3.Bb5 is a well-known Anti-Sicilian that is still pretty common at Master level.

White begins with e4. We'll reply with c5.

2rqkb1r/1b1p1ppp/p3p1n1/1p6/3PP3/2NQ1N2/.text:
We've got an extremely comfortable position after ...Ng6.

Sure, White has kept two pawns in the center, but we've got an active bishop on b7 and a rook on the c-file.

Our dark-squared bishop will come to d6 to try and induce e5 from White, which would make our bishop on b7 even more powerful.

2rqkb1r/1b1pnppp/p3p3/1p6/3PP3/2NQ1N2/PP.text: They can slide the queen to d3, but they've lost a lot of tempi.

r1b1kb1r/1p2nppp/p1n1p3/2pq4/8/2N2N2/PPP.text: Sure, the queen can be a target for one move...

r1bq1rk1/1p1pbppp/p1B1p1n1/8/3NPP2/2N1B3.text:
This was a good moment for it, because White will probably choose to keep the momentum and capture now.

That will give us a lot of active ideas in the center.

Now we've got opportunities to push either ...d5 or ...c5, or both.

Our light-squared bishop will either fianchetto on b7 or develop to a6 in the future.

r1bq1rk1/3pbppp/p1p1p1n1/5P2/3NP3/2N1B3/.text:
White's whole game-plan revolves around f5.

But it's not that big of a threat.

r1bq1rk1/3pbppp/p1p1p3/4nP2/3NP3/2N1B3/P.text:
If anything, it gives us a central square for the knight.

White's attack isn't heading anywhere right now and our ideas remain clear.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pbppp/2n1p1n1/1B6/3NPP2/2N1B.text:
An active idea is f4, expanding on the kingside and in the center.

We don't want White to retain pressure on both sides of the board, so it's time to relieve some of it.

We'll proceed by attacking the bishop on b5.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/2n1p1n1/1B6/3NP3/2N1B3/.text:
They continue natural development instead.

We'll castle and await White's next move.

r1bqkb1r/1p1pnppp/p1n1p3/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
White might have played Re1 to open up the f1-square for it.

But we can contest the center now.

White's setup is rather passive.

r1bqkb1r/1p1pnppp/p1n1p3/2p5/B3P3/2P2N2/.text:
White logically retreats to a4.

But we'll keep chasing the bishop, of course.

This is our main point when White plays it slower.

r1bqkb1r/1p2nppp/p1n1p3/2p5/8/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
But we'll pay that price.

Now our knight is coming to f5, from where it will hardly be attacked but will control d4 and play a role on the kingside.

We can play ...b6 to strengthen the c5-pawn and fianchetto the light-squared bishop as well, while kingside development stays standard.

I prefer this approach to one we would have gotten had we recaptured on d5 with anything else but the queen.

r1bqkb1r/1p2nppp/p1n1p3/2pP4/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
They capture once.

It might seem more logical to recapture with the pawn and keep the central pawns together.

But instead I recommend capturing with the queen!

We've got plans for the knight on f5 and we don't want to open up the e-file and activate White's rook.

r1bqkb1r/3pnppp/p1n1p3/1pp5/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
White retreats to c2, keeping their bishop somewhat active...

And we'll fianchetto ours on b7.

To complete kingside development, we will rotate the knight to g6 which is already a standard idea.

On the queenside, our rook is coming to the c-file at some point.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p1n1/1B6/3NP3/2N5/P.text:
White activates the queenside knight, as well...

And we'll prepare to castle.

Not much confrontation going on right now, as White doesn't want to take on c6 and improve our pawns in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1B6/3NP3/8/PPP2P.text:
The knight arrives at d4, and White's idea is to put even more pressure on our c6-knight.

However, it is sufficiently defended.

Instead of going for queenside operations, we should respond to White's piece activity with our own.

The knight is solid on g6 and opens up the e7-square for further development.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/3PP3/5N2/PP.text:
White can choose to strike in the center now.

This assertive move is also the least popular.

We'll capture, as one should in the Sicilian.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4P3/2P2N2/P.text:
For example, c3 is the most popular move in this position, designed to prepare d4.

It also gives the bishop an escape route.

But time is precious.

We'll strike first by attacking the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Another idea White can implement here is bringing the rook to the center of the board.

This is a slow improving move that gives us time to mix a queenside approach with one in the center.

First of all, we'll attack the bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
And in this study, they don't.

This happens almost 30% of the time, and there are more than 800,000 games in the database like this.

We'll play Nge7 after which there isn't much merit to White capturing, as our kingside knight would replace the queenside one on c6.

Having said that, the bishop on b5 can now become a target for ...a6 and ...b5 expansions.

And if White is slow, even ...d5 could come at some point.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.text:
White goes for the Rossolimo, attacking our knight.

3...e6 is flexible and offers multiple ideas.

The primary one being ...Nge7 if White doesn't capture.

r2qkb1r/1b1pnppp/p1n1p3/1p6/3PP3/5N2/PPB.text:
The pawn recaptures.

This position is more convenient for us when we've already expanded and developed on the queenside and White's bishop is on c2.

Because we can attack it!

Not only is the bishop under attack, but also the e4-pawn, so White doesn't have a lot of wiggle room.

r2qkb1r/1b1pnppp/p1n1p3/1pp5/3PP3/2P2N2/.text:
White keeps their plans alive with d4, though.

We certainly have to be prepared for this move to come at some point.

Let's capture once.

r2qkb1r/1b1pnppp/p3p3/1p6/1n1PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
They will most likely give up the bishop.

Which is certainly a positional victory for us.

r2qkb1r/1b1pnppp/p3p3/1p6/3PP3/2N2N2/PPQ.text:
The queen recaptures, and our position just continues to play itself.

Now the rook comes to the c-file with tempo, threatening ...b4!

White has to defend against our threats again.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Developing the knight to f3.

We'll get our knight behind the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The second study of this chapter will show an alternative for White on move 4 in the Rossolimo.

White doesn't have to capture our knight on c6.

Instead, they can choose to castle and keep their bishop on b5.

To adapt, we'll support our knight with the other one and expand on the queenside, as you will see.

White opens with e4, and we'll reply with c5.

2rq1rk1/pp2n1pp/2n1p3/3p4/1b6/1B3NB1/PP3.text: The other bishop has to retreat as well.

2rq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n1N3/3p4/1b3B2/1B3N2/PP.text:
White has no choice but to capture on e6.

Which opens up our f-rook as well!

It seems like White is helping us activate our pieces with the way they are playing.

2rq1rk1/pp4pp/2n1p3/3p1n2/1b6/1B3NB1/PP3.text:
And now we can enjoy our activity after ...Nf5.

Capturing the bishop on g3 is a good positional idea depending on what White plays.

Our only weakness is the pawn on e6.

If White plays Qe2 to attack it, we can actually place one of the knights on d4 to attack the queen and protect the pawn.

r1b2rk1/pp1pnpp1/2n1p2p/q7/1bB1P2B/2N2N2.text:
White defends against one threat.

But can't really stop our expansion in the center.

r1b2rk1/pp2npp1/2n4p/q2p4/1b5B/1BN2N2/PP.text:
The bishop has to retreat.

Our knight is a little bit loose on e7, although defended.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnpp1/2n1p2p/8/1bB1P2B/2N2N2.text:
White retreats to h4.

How to proceed and fight for ...d5?

The best move is ...Qa5!

We unpin and put more pressure on the knight, all while keeping an eye on d5!

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1N6/1bB1PB2/5N2/.text:
White can try Nb5 with the idea of infiltrating on one of the two dark squares, supported by the bishop.

But we are not afraid. We'll strike in the center with d5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/6B1/1bB1P3/2N2N2.text:
The queen will get developed to e2 at some point.

Now here's our idea.

First, we will attack the bishop with ...h6.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/1bB1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
They can play Rd1, but we'll get what we want anyway.

We'll capture on c3.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/2B1P3/2P2N2/P3.text:
The pawn recaptures.

And now it's time to expand with ...d5!

We aren't actually attacking the bishop right now, but we are aiming for the dangerous ...Qa5 with multiple threats incoming.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n1p3/1N1P4/1bB2B2/5N2/.text:
White captures.

We'll take back, of course.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3P4/2B5/2P2N2/P3Q.text:
White captures once, although that's not the best move.

We'll recapture with the pawn and open up our bishop as a result.

Logical.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/1N1p4/1b3B2/1B3N2/P.text:
The bishop has to retreat.

But now we have all the momentum.

Placing the bishop on e6 not only defends the d5-pawn...

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/3p2B1/2B5/2P2N2/P3Q.text:
A confrontational reply is Bg5, pinning our knight.

We don't want to go ...Qa5 now and abandon our knight, although that could be playable as well.

I suggest we simply consolidate, defend the d-pawn and block the queen's vision of the e-file.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/3p4/1b6/1BN2N2/PP1B.text:
We've got excellent development and no weaknesses, so White's gambit has backfired.

There's not enough compensation.

We do have an IQP in the center of the board which we should protect as much as we can and look to turn into an asset in the future.

If White plays a3, watch out for Nxd5 tactics after ...Ba5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2nppp/2n5/3p4/8/PBP2N2/5PPP/R.text:
But we'll simply bring the king to safety with an easy plan ahead.

Our bishop is coming to e6 to protect the IQP and we'll push ...h6 to restrict White from playing Bg5.

Nothing to fear in this position.

r1bq1rk1/ppb1nppp/2n5/3p4/1PB5/P1N2N2/3B.text:
Now our light-squared bishop is open as well.

White still has to retreat and we'll develop to either f5 or g4 on the next move.

We're doing great.

r1bq1rk1/ppbpnppp/2n1p3/8/1PB1P3/P1N2N2/.text:
White could bring out the queen.

But will have to face our d-pawn advance anyway.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/1bB1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White could unpin immediately, but I would argue that this move is too cautious.

It's slow and gives us everything we need.

Consequently, it's only played 11% of the time.

We'll continue with our standard plan and prepare castling while aiming for ...d5.

White castling is definitely quicker than 7.Bd2 and more resilient.

It's played three quarters of the time.

We still have some developing to do before thinking about ...d5.

Namely, we have to develop the knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/1N6/1bB1P3/5N2/PP.text:
White jumping to b5 on move 8 is a one-move threat.

White simply wants to jump to d6.

This could be a tricky line where White manages to regain the pawn, but not without paying a price.

Now the standard ...d5 defends against Nd6 as well.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/6B1/1bB1P3/2N2N2/.text:
What's certainly a resilient option for White is Bg5, pinning our knight to the queen.

This does temporarily prevent ...d5.

But we'll have other means of fighting against that.

Let's castle first.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/1bB1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
There is no time to waste if White castles.

The bishop on d2 is blocking the queen's vision of the center anyway.

So let's push the critical d-pawn!

The main line and the most common move is Qe2.

White develops the queen and wants to bring the rook to d1 to help out on the d-file.

We'll castle first.

White hasn't done anything about our plan yet.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/1bB1P3/P1N2N2/1.text:
White could attack our bishop and look to expand on the queenside.

No problem.

We'll retreat to a5.

White could go after our bishop immediately.

Since there is no bishop on d2, we will trade.

There was no merit to retreating because we want to neutralize a defender of the d5-square.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/1bB1PB2/2N2N2/P.text:
White could try for Bf4 here.

This comes with the idea of playing on the dark squares around our king.

But doesn't do much about ...d5.

We'll castle first, and you already know what our idea is.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/8/2B1P3/P1P2N2/5P.text:
And once White captures, we get what we wanted.

We can push ...d5!

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/2n1p3/b7/1PB1P3/P1N2N2/.text:
And we've got the c7-square, so our bishop isn't stuck.

It's doing a great job eyeing the kingside from the c7-square.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/1N1P4/1bB5/5N2/PP3.text:
White captures.

And we'll take back.

Our plan, if allowed, is to defend the pawn with ...Be6 next and castle.

But there's a tactic here.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3P4/1bB5/2N2N2/PP1.text:
White takes.

And we'll recapture, renewing the attack.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/3P4/2B5/P1P2N2/5PP.text:
White captures once.

We'll recapture.

The light-squared bishop is now open.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/1N1B4/1b6/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White can capture on d5!

The idea is that once we trade...

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/3p4/1b6/1BN2N2/PP1B1.text: Once it retreats, it's time to hide the king.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n5/3p4/8/PBP2N2/5PPP/R1.text: White has to retreat to b3.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n5/1N1Q4/1b6/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
They can temporarily offer the queen.

This was the other idea of Nb5, though.

If we capture the queen there is Nc7+ getting it right back.

So let's castle instead.

r1bqk2r/ppbpnppp/2n1p3/8/1PB1P3/P1N2N2/3.text:
White castles...

And so will we.

It's not that easy to prevent the incoming ...d5.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/8/2B1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White finishes kingside development and prepares castling.

They've got a lot of pieces covering the center.

As I mentioned, the battle will revolve around d5 and if we manage to push ...d5 at some point, we will be in good shape.

So, ...Bb4 to pin one of the pieces that control that square is logical.

Our knight will also be coming to e7 to support the d5-expansion.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2N2N2/PP3PPP.text:
It's more natural to bring both knights out first.

5.Nf3 is played 63% of the time.

And we'll play ...e6.

But why ...e6 and not ...d6?

Well, our central plan is going to revolve around the d5-square, as you will see.

Pushing ...d5 will give us the central space we need and will allow our pieces to breathe.

r1br2k1/pp3ppp/2n5/1N6/1b6/5N2/PP3PPP/R1.text:
They have won back the pawn, but we have an active rook in the center and most important of all, the bishop pair.

We'll kick out the knight next and finish our queenside development.

White isn't worse according to the computer, but this is probably not a position you want to get out of the opening as White.

r2q1rk1/pp2nppp/2n1b3/3p2B1/8/1BP2N2/P3Q.text:
White finally retreats with the bishop, perhaps anticipating ...Qa5.

But we don't have to play it now.

We can calmly ask the bishop a question instead.

r2q1rk1/ppN1nppp/2n1b3/3p4/1b3B2/1B3N2/P.text:
But also gives us the c8-square for the rook once it's attacked with Nc7!

Our rook is active and attacking the knight.

r2qr1k1/pp2npp1/2n1b2p/3p4/7B/1BP2N2/P3Q.text:
But there's nothing to worry about after ...Re8.

We've managed to push ...d5, consolidate our pieces and defend our weaknesses.

A good plan is to bring out the queen to the queenside next and play ...Nf5 at some point, and our rook is coming to the c- or d-file as well.

Black is always slightly better here, suggesting the Smith-Morra gambit is perhaps not the best choice for White.

r4rk1/pp2npp1/2n1b2p/q2p4/1b5B/1BN2N2/PP.text:
But ...Be6 solves all our problems.

White hasn't managed to stop ...d5 even after pinning our knight with Bg5!

We'll bring the rooks to the center next and enjoy a comfortable game.

If White attacks our bishop with a3, we can even capture on c3.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Usually, the game continues by White playing 2.Nf3 and then going for d4 and a fair trade in the center.

However, in the Smith-Morra White rushes with 2.d4!

This gambit occurs in 8% of all games, which is almost 50 million games in the database!

White has placed both pawns in the center, and we certainly don't want them to stay there.

Therefore we'll capture on d4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/RN.text:
If White recaptures with the queen, it can become a target after ...Nc6.

The point of the Smith-Morra is something else.

White offers another pawn on c3 and wants quick development after we recapture with the knight.

This is played almost half the time.

Declining the gambit is possible here, and there are some transpositions to the c3 Sicilian after e.g. 3...Nf6 4.e5 Nd5.

We'll accept, and try to show that we can survive and be a clear pawn up.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

We don't have anything developed yet, while they've got a pawn in the center and an activated knight.

Is White's lead in development worth the price of a pawn?

It's time for us to start developing, and we'll begin with the queenside knight.

We don't want to play ...Nf6 first and run into e5.

White could play 5.Bc4 here, but after 5...e6 6.Nf3 we would transpose back to the main line.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The Smith-Morra Gambit is an interesting weapon for White against the Sicilian Defense.

It goes against the core purpose of the Sicilian, which is to prevent White from placing both pawns in the center in two moves.

The Smith-Morra challenges this plan directly.

White opens with 1.e4, and we'll reply with 1...c5.

1rbqk1nr/3pppbp/p5p1/1ppB4/3nPP2/2NP1N2/.text:
For now, White connects their pawns.

And we'll attack the bishop.

1rbqk2r/3pnpbp/p3p1p1/1pp5/3nPP2/1BNP1N2.text:
And a standard idea is ...Nge7, with castling to follow.

We can develop the bishop next and play for ...d5.

We've got a space advantage and shouldn't be afraid of the trade on d4.

If White captures on d4 now, it might be better to recapture with the bishop.

r1b1k2r/pp1pppbp/1q4p1/1B1nP3/3p1P2/8/PP.text:
We've got ...Qb6 with multiple threats.

We are attacking the bishop but also threatening ...d3+ with check and an attack on the knight.

The only way to save a piece is Bd3, but White is still in an uncomfortable spot after ...Nb4.

r1b1k2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/qB6/3pPP2/3P4/PPP1.text:
An simple fork.

Black is winning.

r1bq1rk1/p3npbp/4p1p1/1p6/3pPP2/1B6/PPP1.text:
Why did we make these trades?

Well, we've still got a lot of central control, but now our bishop can be activated to b7.

A good plan is to continue pushing on the queenside with ...a5.

White might push e5, and although that blocks one of our bishops, it strengthens the other one.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pnpbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2B1PP2/2NP.text:
A good plan to counteract our central expansion is to try and play on the dark squares on the kingside.

White might want to push f5 and bring the queen to h4, and follow it up with Bh6.

Let's not give them time to go through with this plan.

We'll strike first.

White capturing on d5 would only open up our light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2n1p1p1/2pp4/4PP2/1BNP1.text:
So they retreat to b3 instead.

Let's continue dominating the center.

We'll go after the bishop and basically force White to trade the knights on d4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/4p1p1/2pp4/3NPP2/1BNP4/.text:
White captures.

It's okay to double our pawns for a moment, because it comes with tempo.

And we'll undouble them right away.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/4p1p1/3p4/3pPP2/1B1P4/P.text:
White retreats to e2.

But now we'll capture on e4.

This is good because White doesn't even have the chance to recapture with the queen now.

And our d4-pawn is defended.

r1bqk1nr/1p1pppbp/p5p1/2p5/2BnPP2/2N2N2/.text:
White retreats to c4 with an idea of their own.

We'll attack it again with b5.

r1bqk1nr/3pppbp/p5p1/1ppB4/3nPP2/2N2N2/P.text:
White wanted to place the bishop on d5 and attack our rook!

The most natural square to move to is b8.

This plan might have been premature from White, however.

The bishop will be a target once again after ...e6.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2B1PP2/2N2.text:
White castles.

There isn't much they can do to stop our plan.

We'll develop the knight first to support the d5-push.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/1Bp5/4PP2/2N2N2/.text:
The most common move in this position is 5.Bb5, played 40% of the time.

White often mixes f4 ideas with Bb5, attacking our knight on c6 which controls key dark central squares.

And the bishop is not susceptible to ...d5 when it's on b5.

We won't give White the chance to capture on c6, as we'll centralize it immediately and create some tension in the center.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2B1PP2/2N2N2.text:
5.Bc4 is played just over 35% of the time, and gives us room to implement some of our Rossolimo ideas.

When the bishop is on c4, ...d5 is a good idea to expand in the center and target it! We'll prepare this with e6.

Our bishop is controlling the dark squares while our pawns will complement this on the light squares.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/1B6/3pPP2/8/PPPPN1.text:
White jumps to e2, which leaves the e4-pawn undefended.

So it's logical to develop and attack it.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/1Bp5/3NPP2/2N5/PPP.text:
White could also choose to capture in the center, but they have to be careful.

If they're not accurate, things might go downhill for them.

We'll recapture with an attack on the knight.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/1Bp5/3nPP2/2N2N2/P.text:
It's probably safest for White to castle here.

We could capture the bishop on b5, but why not use the chance and expand on the queenside instead?

We can make the bishop a target while we advance our pawns.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2B1PP2/2NP1.text:
And White opens up the dark-squared bishop and connects the pawn chain.

We don't have to rush with ...d5.

It's coming anyway.

It's safer to hide our king first.

White can't stop ...d5, but they still have plans of their own.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/1B2P3/3p1P2/8/PPPP.text:
The most sensible move is pushing the pawn to e5.

No problem.

We'll put the knight in the center and still get some pressure.

White shouldn't trade the f4-pawn for the d4-pawn.

It would break apart their pawn chain.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/1B6/3pPP2/3P4/PPP1.text: Defending the pawn with d3 loses a piece.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/1B1nP3/3p1P2/8/PPPP.text: And castling is a mistake, too.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2p5/4PP2/2N2N2/P.text:
White continues by developing the knight.

Logical.

And we'll complete the fianchetto.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4PP2/2N5/PPPP2.text:
Here, White goes for 3.Nf3 most of the time, transposing to main Sicilian variations - but we'll analyze 3.f4 here.

It's played 20% of the time.

White looks for kingside expansion before developing the knight to f3, and often wants to attack by pushing f5 at some point.

I recommend the fianchetto setup to stay solid.

Not only will our bishop be strong on g7 since White isn't playing d4, but the g6-pawn also controls the f5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
Already, 2.Nc3 is a deviation to the main lines, which is a signal that White might go for an Anti-Sicilian.

This move develops a piece but leaves White's options open for pushing the f-pawn before Nf3.

It's played 9% of the time, which is still almost 55 million games in the database!

We'll continue with the natural developing move Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In Chapter 3, we'll take a look at the Grand Prix Attacks by White.

They are characterized by the moves 2.Nc3 and either 3.f4 or moving the bishop on move 3.

White wants an alternative expansion to d4 and often tries to attack quickly on the kingside.

White opens with e4.

We'll go for the Sicilian.

r1b1k1nr/1p2ppbp/p5p1/3q4/3p4/3B4/PPPPNP.text:
We'll develop the bishop.

Our knight is coming to f6 next and we'll castle.

If White continues attacking the pawn with something like b3 and Bb2, we can play ...Nh6 instead so that our bishop can always defend d4. 

From h6, the knight has f5 and g4.

r1bqk1nr/1p2p1bp/p4Pp1/3p4/3p1P2/3B4/PPP.text:
White captures.

They didn't have much of a choice.

We'll recapture with the knight and develop it.

White has to be careful here.

r1bqk1nr/1p2ppbp/p5p1/3pP3/3p1P2/3B4/PPP.text:
White's idea is to try and keep the pawns on e5 and f4.

But it's not going to be that easy.

We'll chip away at the structure immediately with f6.

r1bqk2r/1p2p1bp/p4np1/3p4/3N1P2/3B4/PPPP.text:
Capturing on d4 loses the game.

Things aren't always as they seem.

r1bqk2r/1p2p1bp/p5p1/3p3n/3N1P2/3B4/PPPP.text:
We've got ...Nh5 with multiple attacks on White's weak points.

Also, ...e5 is coming if something like Ne2, which would give us a lot of activity.

White is in trouble.

r1bqk2r/1p2ppbp/p4np1/8/8/2P2B2/P2PNPPP/.text:
And now our bishop is finally active on g7, and we'll castle next.

A trade of bishops on g4 at some point is not a bad idea, if our pawn on b7 is protected.

If that happens, we can solidify our position with ...e6.

r1bqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/p3pn2/2p5/P1BnP3/2N5/1.text:
White stops one pawn expansion...

But not the other. We'll push in the center.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3nn2/2pp4/P7/2N5/BPPPNP.text:
So we'll keep the knight safe and the center strong.

Our bishop is coming to d6 next and we'll castle.

We also may think of ...Bb8 to create a battery with our queen.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pP4/P1Bn4/2N5/1PP.text:
White takes on d5.

We'll recapture with the pawn and reinstate our attack on the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p4n2/2pp4/P2n4/2N5/BPPPN.text:
White retreats to a2 now.

Since they captured on d5 with the e-pawn, we might want to avoid the trade on d4 now.

It would double our pawns and open up the e-file.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BnP3/2N5/PPP.text:
Instead, they castle.

Which gives us more flexibility on the light squares.

Apart from ...d5, we also want ...b5.

r1bqkbnr/1p1ppp1p/p5p1/2p5/3NP3/2NB4/PPP.text:
White trades.

They want to double our pawns either way.

We'll recapture with an attack on the knight...

r1bqkbnr/1p1ppp1p/p5p1/8/3pP3/3B4/PPPPNP.text:
Which retreats to e2, attacking our pawn.

We could play ...Bg7 and protect it, but I recommend something much more active.

Now that the white knight has stepped back, we can play ...d5!

We can afford to push this central pawn because White can't capture on d4.

If they do, we've got ...dxe4 with a double attack.

r1bqkbnr/1p1ppppp/p7/2p5/3nP3/2NB1N2/PPP.text:
They retreat to d3 instead, but now their d-pawn is blocked in.

I recommend a fianchetto approach here.

...d5 is not currently possible, but on g7 our bishop will be controlling the key dark squares on the long diagonal.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pp1p/p5p1/3P4/3p4/3B4/PPPPNP.text:
Capturing on d5 isn't scary at all.

We'll just recapture with the queen and keep our pawn protected.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pp1p/p5p1/3p4/3pP3/2PB4/PP1P.text:
They can undermine our pawn on d4 instead.

Let's capture on e4 first and get rid of our doubled pawns.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pp1p/p5p1/3pP3/3p4/3B4/PPPPN.text:
Keeping the center closed can be achieved after e5.

This move looks weird but White wants to play on the dark squares against our bishop.

We've already committed to the fianchetto, so Bg7 makes sense here.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pp1p/p5p1/8/3pB3/2P5/PP1PNPP.text:
White recaptures.

Now we'll take on c3 as well.

Much more practical than protecting our pawn.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pp1p/p5p1/8/4B3/2P5/P2PNPPP/.text:
White recaptures.

Why did we make these two trades and open up the center?

Because we can develop with tempo and castle quickly.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p5/2BnP3/2N5/PPPP.text:
White activates the knight to e2 and offers a trade.

For now, we'll focus on development.

We don't mind White capturing on d4 as that would dislodge their knight on c3 and allow us to capture on e4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/1Bp5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1.text:
A move that's played 10% of the time is Bb5, but I believe it deserves more coverage than 3.Bc4.

White has a more direct idea here: pressuring our knight and fighting for the d4-square.

I suggest we jump to d4 immediately.

With this move, we get the knight out of the way, attack the bishop on b5, and prevent d4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/1Bp5/3nP3/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
A somewhat trickier move than Bc4 is Nf3.

White calls our bluff and keeps the bishop on b5, offering a trade of knights.

Instead of capturing the bishop, we'll make it a target for our queenside expansion.

If White moves to a4, their bishop will get trapped.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/2BnP3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
White might think our main idea was to capture on b5 and thus retreat to c4.

We'll go for ...e6 to play for ...d5 at some point.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight.

A flexible move.

We'll prevent any possible d4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of the Grand Prix chapter, we'll take a look at setups with 2.Nc3 and White moving the light-squared bishop on move 3, to either c4 or b5.

Instead of 3.f4, White wants to put pressure on our position early by implementing a mixed development approach with one kingside and one queenside piece.

White opens with e4 and we'll reply with the Sicilian.

1rbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n5/2pNb3/8/3P2P1/P1P1NP.text:
After we take care of our b7-pawn, we have managed to keep the bishop pair which is an important factor in the middlegame and the endgame.

White does have the b-file but their pawns are split and the a2-pawn could be a target.

We can continue by improving our pieces and perhaps playing ...b6.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4PP2/6P1/PPP3.text:
It seems like this position is harmless without the queens, but we can spice things up.

An active move is to jump to d4 and threaten a fork on c2.

The best move for White is in fact Kd2.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/3nPPN1/6P1/PPP3B.text:
White should accept the sacrifice and allow the fork.

We'll capture on c2, of course.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/4PPN1/6P1/PP4BP/.text:
And we'll take the rook in the corner.

It's important to make sure the knight escapes from a1 because we don't want to give up both knights for the rook.

We will accomplish that by placing the bishop on b5 or a4 and restricting the king. The rook is coming to d8 as well.

If White plays b3 now with Bb2 as an idea, you have ...c4.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3nPP2/4N1P1/PPP.text:
Ne3 looks more natural, but now we have a tactic.

And that's to try and deflect the knight from guarding c2!

White is suddenly tangled up and it's hard to defend everything.

Kd1 doesn't work because of ...Nf2+.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2B2/2p5/3p4/2NP2P1/PP.text:
White throws in this capture to avoid the trade on e4.

We'll recapture.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2pp2B1/8/2NP2P1/P.text:
White castles as well.

This is a good opportunity to play ...d4 to dislodge the knight on c3 which now doesn't have a square on e2.

This destabilizes White's position.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n5/2p5/3pNN2/3P2P1/PPP.text:
White continues improving their pieces.

We'll play on the light squares and bring our bishop to f5.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2b2/2p5/3pN3/3P2P1/PPP.text:
And the knight finds itself on e4, attacking our bishop.

We shouldn't let White capture.

Let's slide back to e7 instead and defend the pawn on c5.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb4/2p5/3pB3/3P2P1/PPP1.text:
As do we. We've managed to dominate the dark squares in the center, and now have a space advantage.

Our rook will occupy the e-file next and we'll solidify the knight with ...Bd7.

White can't really take on c6, as the white squares around the king would become weak.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4NP2/3P2P1/PP.text:
But we'll just defend our knight on f6 and continue with moves like ...Qc7 and ...b6, followed by the fianchetto on b7.

We want to defend the queenside and then fight on the diagonal.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2B2/2pp4/8/2NP2P1/PPP2.text:
White can definitely capture on f6.

What will happen is a trade of pawns.

We'll recapture with the bishop.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2pp2B1/8/2NP2P1/PP.text:
Instead of taking advantage of that,  White can go for development now.

We'll castle before anything else.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n2b2/2pN4/8/3P2P1/PPP2PB.text:
White does take in the center...

But we get the b2-pawn with an attack on the rook.

This is a fair trade because we eliminate White's pawn majority on the queenside while their center is still weak.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n5/2pN4/8/3P2P1/PbP2PBP/.text:
The rook gets a tempo back on our bishop.

But we'll retreat to the center of the board.

We don't want to go back to f6 and allow White to capture.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n5/2pNb3/8/3P2P1/P1P1NPB.text:
They develop, preparing to castle.

We'll get our king into safety.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4P3/2NP2P1/.text:
We will cover 5.d3 in Study 1.

White simply opens up the bishop on c1 to join the fight on the dark squares.

It's played almost half the time, in 240,000 games.

We'll waste no time but strike in the center immediately.

Let's see how White can respond.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/2p5/4P3/2N3P1/PP.text:
White goes for the fianchetto.

And we prepare to neutralize that bishop with ...d5 in the future.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/3pP3/2NP2P1/P.text:
The reason is that it's too passive and gives us space to push ...d4.

Now the knight on c3 doesn't have any comfortable squares to go to.

In fact, it should probably retreat to b1.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4PP2/2N3P1/PP.text:
Recapturing with the pawn allows us to trade queens.

We'll take White up on their offer.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pP4/8/2NP2P1/PPP.text:
The most common move is White simply capturing in the center, and it is played 40% of the time.

White removes some of the tension and gives their bishop a little bit of breathing room.

We'll continue to control the center with our d5-pawn. 

In this way, we create a block for the bishop on g2. It cannot see past our pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/4P3/2NP2P1/P.text:
Developing the knight to e2 now is an inaccuracy.

It's played 15% of the time.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/4PP2/2NP2P1/.text:
White goes for f4 almost 20% of the time.

It's a logical expansion now that they've already developed some of the pieces.

Going for ...d4 is playable here but I don't want to open their bishop on g2.

Let's take in the center instead.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2p5/3pN3/3P2P1/PPP.text:
The knight will probably jump to e4.

Let's trade.

White's knight is more active than ours.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2pp2B1/8/2NP2P1/PP.text:
A sensible move you should look out for is Bg5.

White targets one of the defenders of the d5-pawn.

We'll defend and unpin.

But did we allow White to remove a defender of the pawn and capture in the center?

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2pp4/8/2NP2P1/PPP1.text:
Once again, the early Nge2 allows us to push.

Which we'll gladly do.

Although we open up White's bishop, we restrict their position and we have a clear plan ahead.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n5/2p5/3pB3/3P2P1/PPP1N.text:
The bishop recaptures.

And we'll finally finish kingside development.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
And now White plays 3.g3, with the idea of Bg2. 10% of games feature this move, which is close to 2.5 million games.

We could argue that this is more "mature" than 3.Bc4 or 3.Bb5.

We'll develop the knight either way.

3...g6 is the main (and strong) option but 3...Nf6 is very straightforward.

As in many of the positions we cover in this course, we'll play on the light squares against White's bishop.

r4rk1/pp1qbppp/2n5/2p2b2/3pNN2/3P2P1/PPP.text:
And we'll line up the queen with the bishop.

If White's knight moves away from f4, you can offer a trade on h3.

Don't be afraid of Qh5. You have ...Nb4, or even ...Bg4.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the queenside knight first.

We'll develop our knight, too.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Let's turn to the Closed Sicilian in this chapter.

It also begins with 1.e4 c5 2.Nc3, but White doesn't go for the explosive 3.f4 or the light-squared bishop action.

Instead, White wants to play positionally with moves like g3, Bg2 and, in this study, d3.

White opens with e4 and we'll reply with c5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4P3/2N3P1/P.text:
White chooses 5.Nge2 just over 35% of the time.

As mentioned, the plan is d4.

We'll play ...d5 anyway.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1pn2/2p5/4PP2/2N3P1/.text:
Played only 8% of the time, f4 is certainly an active-looking move that aims to play e5 at some point.

However, if we're quick with central counterplay, there's nothing to be afraid of.

Let's strike in the center before White gets the chance to play e5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/2p5/4P3/2N3P1/PP.text:
The fianchetto prompts us to push...

The e-pawn, preparing ...d5.

r1bqkb1r/pp3pp1/2n1p2n/2ppP2p/5P2/2N2NP1.text:
And it's time to develop our knight again.

It's coming to f5 from where it will control the d4-square.

Our bishop is coming to e7 as well.

The conclusion is that White hasn't achieved much playing like this and will have to resort to d3 now.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pP4/8/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
White captures.

And we'll keep our pawns in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2ppP3/5P2/2N3P1/P.text:
They can do it now, but our pawn is already on d5.

There is nothing wrong with bringing the knight back to g8.

White has committed their pawns and won't be able to push further.

Since they've overextended a bit, there is space for our knight on f5 now.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P4/2N3P1/PPP.text:
Once d4 comes, White has declared war.

There will be a lot of fighting around this square.

It's most natural to take.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N4/2N3P1/PPP2.text:
The knight recaptures.

And here's a strong move to keep in mind.

It's ...Bg4, attacking the queen!

The g-knight is already on d4 and it's a little bit uncomfortable for White to deal with this.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/2N3P1/PPPP.text:
White goes for g3.

The bishop is coming to g2.

We'll develop both knights.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/5P2/2N2NP1/P.text:
White continues with kingside development.

And I suggest ...h5 before ...Nh6.

We simply prevent g4 and grab some space.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N4/2N2PP1/PPP.text:
And normal development will follow.

We'll castle short and bring the rooks to e8 and c8.

We do have an isolated pawn on d5 which White will probably attack, so playing around it is a good idea.

White still has to spend some moves bringing the light-squared bishop back to life.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2bp4/3N2b1/2NQB1P1/P.text:
They protect the knight instead.

But we're not done applying pressure.

The queen is a great piece to help out the bishop.

It attacks the pawn on b2 as well so White's hand is pretty much forced.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N2b1/2N2PP1/PP.text:
A move you can expect to see frequently here is f3.

Although we have to move the bishop again, White has blocked their own bishop.

We'll retreat to d7 where it's safest.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3N2b1/2NQ2P1/PP.text:
White could choose to move the queen instead of blocking the attack.

It's time to fight for d4.

We'll begin by pressuring the knight.

We're happy if White captures, as our pawn on d5 would no longer be isolated.

r3k2r/p4ppp/2p2n2/3p4/6b1/2N1P1P1/PPP3BP.text:
Why did we make all these trades?

Well, our center is now compact again and White has a serious weakness on e3 which we will be able to play against.

Their plan might have backfired.

There are some lines where you don't even have to castle.

In any case, bringing the rooks to the center and/or occupying the b-file is a good plan.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qN2n2/2bp4/6b1/2NQB1P1/PPP.text:
They have to relieve some tension.

We'll take on e3 first and trade everything.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/1qN2n2/3p4/6b1/2N1Q1P1/PPP2.text:
White recaptures with the queen and gives a check.

We'll trade again.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
Developing the knight.

We'll do the same.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The second study of this chapter will look at 5.Nge2 and 5.f4 from White.

The purpose of 5.Nge2 is for White to prepare the active d4 instead of the more solid d3.

On the other hand, 5.f4 leads to dark-squared play where White wants to grab space quickly and dislodge our knight from f6.

The game starts with e4. We'll respond with c5.

3rk2r/pp2ppbp/2nqb1p1/3n4/2BP4/1QN2N2/PP.text:
And we'll complete the fianchetto.

Now we are the ones attacking, since our knight is sufficiently defended.

Trading on d5 only helps us play against the isolated pawn.

If White goes for something like Ne4, we can slide the queen to c7.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/2nq2p1/3n4/2BP4/2N2N2/P.text:
White brings the bishop to c4, attacking our knight.

Again, we should avoid the trade on c3.

We can protect the knight instead with Be6.

Now taking on c3 is an actual threat, since it would come with a discovered attack on the bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2nq4/3n4/3P4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
And that's exactly what we will do when White plays Nc3.

Of course, we don't want to capture and fix their pawn structure.

We'll go for ...g6 with the idea of ...Bg7 instead.

r1bQkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/4P3/1nB5/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
Sure, they can trade the queens.

We'll capture with the knight and retain our castling rights.

There is still the threat of ...Nc2+.

r1bQkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/4P3/8/2n2N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White trades queens.

We'll recapture with the knight.

We want to keep castling rights.

r1bnkb1r/1p2pppp/p7/4P3/1nB5/N4N2/PP3PPP.text:
White finally castles.

Let's develop the light-squared bishop before ...e6.

r1bnkb1r/pp2pppp/8/4P3/1nB5/N4N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White defends it with Na3.

Perhaps Nb5 or Bb5+ is a counter threat.

Which is why ...a6 makes sense here.

r1bnkb1r/pp2pppp/8/4P3/8/2P2N2/P4PPP/R1B.text:
Finally, White recaptures on c3, but now that pawn is a clear target.

It's isolated.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/3nN3/2BP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
And we'll develop the dark-squared bishop as well, preparing castling next.

White hasn't accomplished anything playing like this.

We can let them trade on c6. I advise against capturing the knight on e5 and bringing their pawns back together.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3nN3/2BP4/8/PP3PPP/.text:
White could take with the knight, but that leaves them with an isolated pawn once again and no real hope for advantage.

We can keep everything solid with ...e6.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3nP3/2B5/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White can recapture and reinstate the attack, but we have something planned.

And that's to move the knight to b4!

We offer a trade of queens but some knight infiltrations are now in the air.

White has to tread carefully.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3nP3/8/2N2N2/PP3PPP.text:
White takes with the pawn.

And now I suggest taking on c3 as well.

This provokes a trade of queens but more importantly, it weakens the c3-pawn in the long run.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/4P3/1nB5/1Q3N2/PP3P.text:
Moving the queen to b3 and avoiding the trade is a dynamic option here.

The f7-pawn is under attack.

We'll cover it with ...e6.

We would like to play ...Na5 at some point and fork the White queen and bishop.

On the other hand, White wants to attack our knight on b4 and play on the light squares.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2nP4/3n4/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
Capturing on d6 here isn't a problem either.

We'll take with the queen and keep our pawns together.

When you see an isolated pawn on d4 in positions like this, you should play for the fianchetto.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PP3P.text:
It looks sensible to play Bc4 and attack our knight at some point.

We'll take in the center, so that our knight is defended.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/3nP3/3P1P2/5N2/PP4.text:
White defends.

We'll take in the center once.

We don't want to give White the option of taking on d6.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np4/3nP3/3P4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White can develop the knight before capturing on d6.

This is different because usually we wouldn't want to take on c3 and connect their pawns.

But here, we'll make some positional trades.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/4P3/1nB5/1Q3N2/PP3.text:
White doesn't have to rush with anything.

They can castle first.

We'll use the opportunity to fork them.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/4P3/1nB5/PQ3N2/1P3.text:
White can attack our knight with a3 right away.

But we have an intermezzo.

We'll fork the two pieces with our knight.

White doesn't exactly have to give up the bishop...

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/n3P3/QnB5/P4N2/1P3PP.text:
They can check on a4.

11.Bb5+ can lead to the same continuation that we'll see here.

The idea is that once we block with the bishop...

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/nB2P3/1n6/1Q3N2/PP3P.text:
This provokes a check on the diagonal.

The only correct piece to block with is the bishop.

Now there's tension between the bishops and the queen on b3 is still under attack.

Apart from that, we are still eyeing the jump to c2!

r2nkb1r/1p2pppp/p7/4P3/1nB3b1/N4N2/PP3PP.text:
We're pressuring the knight on f3 and will follow up with ...e6 and ...Nc6 to attack the e5-pawn.

White's pieces are slightly misplaced and we have an easy position to play.

r2nkb1r/pp1bpppp/8/4P3/8/2P2N2/P4PPP/R1B.text:
And we'll develop the light-squared bishop.

Depending on what White plays, we can be flexible with our bishop and place it on either e7 or g7.

The knight is coming to c6 and the rook to c8.

The point is to pressure White's loose pawns on e5 and c3 with everything we've got.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/nB2P3/8/P4N2/1PQ2PP.text:
So they capture.

But now we capture on b5 and suddenly all our problems are solved.

There is no tension on the diagonal anymore and we're preventing White from castling.

The rook is coming to c8 to help out as well.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/nB2P3/Qn6/5N2/PP3PP.text:
The only move that doesn't lose the game is Qa4.

We'll trade once.

We don't want White to trade on d7 on their own terms.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4p3/nB2P3/Qn6/P4N2/1P3P.text:
They can bring their own to b5.

White has a lot of pressure and they are threatening to trade on d7 and then capture on b4.

But we can solve these problems by giving a check on c2!

This gives up the knight but deflects the queen from the bishop's defense.

White has to take the knight, otherwise they'd lose the rook on a1.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3nP3/3P2b1/5N2/PP4PP.text:
And our idea is to pin the knight on f3.

It's the one piece that holds everything together for White.

Next, we'll play ...e6 and get the bishop out to prepare castling.

In the long run, the idea is to play against the d4-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1Q2P3/1n6/2N2N2/PP3.text:
The best move is Nc3, opening up the b1-square for the rook if needed.

Let's kick the queen away.

White doesn't have many comfortable squares to retreat to.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/nQ2P3/1n6/5N2/PP3PPP/.text:
The queen recaptures with check.

It's better to block with the a-knight because we keep our main threat active, and that's ...Nc2.

Now ...a6 is an idea as well.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/nb2P3/8/P1N2N2/1PQ2PP.text:
A natural move like Nc3 makes things even worse for White...

Because we can offer a queen trade with Qd3.

r3kb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/4P3/1n6/2Nq1N2/PP2Q.text:
But we'll go for this trade.

We want the queens off the board because it will gives us a lot of light-squared presence for the knights.

The position is still equal but we've got some momentum and the e5-pawn could become weak in an ending.

r3kb1r/pp2pp1p/2nqb1p1/3n4/2BP4/1QN2N2/P.text:
So White brings the queen to b3.

The queen is acting as an attacker and a defender at the same time.

Luckily, we can bring the rook to d8 and continue defending.

White can't capture on b7 because of the tactic on c3.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/n3P3/8/P1Nb1N2/1P3PPP/.text:
Why was the queen trade beneficial for us?

The queen was the only piece covering the holes on the light squares in White's position, which are now accessible.

Apart from that, we've kept the bishop pair and are clearly better.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pp1p/3q2p1/3n4/3P4/2N5/PP3PP.text:
And I suggest we fianchetto on g7.

From there, the bishop will make the d4-pawn a permanent target.

We'll continue pressuring it with ...Nc6, as well.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/3q4/3n4/3P4/2N5/PP3PPP/.text: White brings out the knight in the hope of us trading on c3.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p1P3/8/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
The most common move is e5.

White takes more space with tempo and attacks our knight...

Forcing it to move again.

The d5-square is best.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
In this chapter, White will play d4 on move 4, and this happens three quarters of the time.

It seems like White got what they wanted.

But it's not that simple.

We'll capture in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/3nP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
White recaptures 70% of the time.

They do have a strong central presence at the moment, which is what we need to focus on.

So it's smart to undermine their structure right away with d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3P4/3n4/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
Capturing on d6 is great for us because it leaves White with an isolated pawn on d4.

We'll recapture with the queen and keep our pawns connected.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P1P2/8/PP4PP/.text:
White could try to hold on to their big pawn center here.

But this might make their position unstable in the long run.

Let's develop the other knight and target the central pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p4/3nP3/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
Nf3, defending the center with the knight, occurs most frequently.

They don't want an IQP after taking on d6 or to overextend with f4.

We'll add some pressure to the central pawns with Nc6.

If instead 6.Bc4 we can just play ...Nb6.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
The Alapin aims for two pawns in the center as early as move 3.

It's only played 5% of the time, which is in almost 29 million games.

There are a couple of ways to deal with this. 2...d5 is one of the main lines.

But I recommend 2...Nf6.

Our knight attacks the e4-pawn and White can't play Nc3 to defend it because there's already a pawn on c3!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The Alapin is an ambitious Anti-Sicilian that White can play, which places a pawn on c3 as early as move two to support a future d4.

That comes with some of its own disadvantages which we will try to exploit in the upcoming studies.

This study will begin with the main lines and White capturing on d4 on move 5.

First, though, we'll get started with White playing 1.e4 and our reply of 1...c5.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/3P4/1B3N2/PP3PP.text:
If White takes on d4 here, it's a little bit different because they have an IQP on d4 which they might want to push to d5.

Now ...Bg4 runs into a common trick: Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+!

So let's place the bishop on e6 instead and cover the d5-square, offering a trade.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3P.text:
If White castles, we have to be a little bit careful.

...Bg4 runs into Bxf7+ here, followed by Ng5+ getting the piece back.

It's better to offer a trade of light-squared bishops.

We would much rather play ...e6 after the bishops are traded than block in our bishop on c8.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/4P3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP.text:
White retreats to b3.

It's important to understand how our setups change in this variation.

We will go for the quick ...d5!

This is more powerful than ...d6 because if White doesn't capture en passant, we'll have a strong pawn in the center blocking White's structure and undermining their bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n5/3nP3/2Bp4/2P2N2/PP.text:
We do have to react if the bishop puts pressure on our knight, though.

Let's bring it to b6 and attack the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/3pP3/3P4/1B3N2/PP3.text:
Capturing on d4 makes our position easy to play.

We'll just develop the bishop before we play ...e6.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nnP4/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3P.text:
If White captures en passant, we get the same position as we would have had we played ...d6 instead of ...d5.

You already know it's better to recapture with the queen from the last study.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/3pP3/3P2b1/1B2BN2/P.text: White reinforces the pawn on d4.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/1nn1p3/3pP3/3P2b1/1B2BN2/.text:
But we have an easy plan ahead after ...e6.

Our bishop is coming to e7 and we'll castle, with a strong center countering White's expansions.

The position is equal but White has no chances for an advantage here.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nn1q3/8/3N4/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
White finally gets the pawn back.

Trading on d4 would give their queen a lot of activity.

We'll retreat to d7 and occupy the d-file instead.

The idea is ...e6 and ...Be7, as per usual.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/1N6/8/1bp2N2/PP2QPP.text:
White can throw in this attacking move.

But if we know that the b8-square is actually fine for the queen, there is nothing to fear.

The queen stays on the dark-squared diagonal which is important.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqB3/8/3p4/2P2N2/PP3PPP.text:
If White captures, it's straightforward.

We'll recapture with the queen to keep our pawn structure intact.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/3P4/1B3N2/PP3PPP.text:
White castles.

And we'll trade.

White's bishop on b3 was a problematic piece, and our bishop was blocking the e6-square.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/3p4/NBP2N2/PP3PP.text:
If White really knows what they're doing, they could try this tricky idea with Na3.

The knight wants to come to b5 at some point.

But White's main idea is, that once we take on c3 and offer a queen trade...

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnqb3/8/8/NBp2N2/PP2QPPP.text:
They avoid it with Qe2, gambiting a pawn!

The threats are Rd1 and Nb5, so we have to be accurate here.

Capturing on b2 is way too dangerous.

Let's trade the bishops first.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nq5/8/8/2P5/PP3PPP/RNBQ1.text:
It's better to keep the queens on the board and the pawns together.

We have the same ideas incoming.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1nnqp3/8/3P4/1Q3N2/PP3PPP/.text:
We can push ...e6 now, with the idea of ...Be7 and ...O-O down the line.

We will be playing against the isolated pawn, but won't rush into capturing it.

We don't want to let White develop with tempo and make some threats before we castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p1P3/8/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
White pushes the e-pawn.

It's best to centralize the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
White goes for the big center.

We'll take.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/3nP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3PP.text:
And now comes Nf3, with White prioritizing development. The purpose of this move is often to follow up with Bc4 and castle short.

Of course, we can't capture on c3 because of our knight on d5.

It's played 18% of the time, in almost 300,000 games.

The alternative of 5.cxd4 would take us back to Study 1.

After Nf3, we'll play the standard ...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
The Alapin variation.

White wants d4.

We'll attack the pawn on e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
The second study will show us how to fight against White's setups with 5.Nf3 in the Alapin.

Instead of recapturing in the center right away, White takes advantage of our pawn being pinned and wants to develop quickly on the kingside.

Let's get started with 1.e4 c5.

rq2kb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/1N6/8/1Pp2N2/1P2QPP.text:
White finally recaptures.

It might seem natural to play ...e6 now and keep our position solid.

rq2kb1r/pp3ppp/1nn5/1N2p3/8/1Pp2N2/1P2QP.text:
But I suggest the more aggressive ...e5!

We have the same kingside ideas, but White will probably have to spend a move recapturing on c3.

We'll get some time with ...a6 and quickly bring the rooks to the center after we castle.

2k2b1r/pp3ppp/1nn5/4p2b/8/2P2N1P/PP3PP1/.text:
And one benefit of trading is that we get to expand in the center with ...e5.

A good plan to move forward is ...Be7 followed by ...Rd8 to improve the pieces on the kingside.

We can also play ...Nc4 and strengthen our center with ...f6.

2kr1b1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/7b/8/2P2N1P/PP2BPP1.text:
The rook recaptures.

We'll swap the rooks as well.

2kr1b1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/7b/8/2P2N1P/PP2BPP.text:
The bishop has to retreat.

And now we can trade everything on the d-file.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nn5/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBPKP.text:
And now we can conveniently develop the knight, with the pawns coming to the dark squares.

An easy position to play.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBP1.text:
And once castling arrives, we can continue with natural development.

It's important to keep in mind that we've successfully prevented d4, which is the main benefit for us when White plays like this.

Now we want to develop the c8-bishop before playing ...e6: we'll do this by placing it on g4, pinning the knight on f3.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/2p1P3/8/1BP2N2/PP.text:
And once it retreats to b3...

We'll push the c-pawn and attack it again.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1nn5/4P3/2p5/2P2N2/PPB.text:
White has to move to c2.

Remember that White won't be able to defend their e5-pawn with another pawn, though.

So we can undermine the center now.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n5/2pnP3/2B5/2P2N2/PP.text:
White can combine their approach with Bc4, on the other hand.

But we have an answer for that, as well.

And our initial response will be similar to the lines after 4.Bc4.

We'll retreat the knight and attack the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/1nnP4/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBP1.text:
White takes.

Our queen will recapture.

r3k2r/pp2bppp/1nnqp3/7b/2p5/NPP2N1P/P1BP.text:
Now if White wants to induce us to take on b3, they have to place the knight on a3, which is far from an optimal square.

Only now will we take and relieve the tension.

r3k2r/pp2bppp/1nnqp3/7b/8/NPP2N1P/2BP1PP.text:
White recaptures with the pawn, and the clear idea is d4 now.

We won't be able to stop it, but we will be able to exploit some weaknesses White has created.

Let's castle first.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/7b/2p5/2P2N1P/PPBP1.text:
Instead of the central approach, White can opt for Re1 here.

The idea is to undermine our c4-pawn with b3 instead of d4.

We'll play ...e6 anyway.

We aren't afraid of b3.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/7b/2pP4/2P2N1P/PPB2.text:
If d4 comes at any point...

We'll just take en passant.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/7b/8/2PB1N1P/PP3PP1.text:
White can trade the queens here, but could also choose to recapture with the bishop.

It might seem like this avoids trading, but it will actually lead to even more trades soon.

Because we will castle long and target the white pieces along the d-file.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1nnq4/8/2p3b1/2P2N1P/PPBP.text:
White attacks it with h3.

Let's slide back to h5 and keep an eye on the knight.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1nnqp3/7b/2p5/1PP2N1P/P1BP.text:
White plays b3, but our pawn on c4 is defended by the knight, so we don't have to take on b3 for now.

We can finish kingside development instead.

r4rk1/1p2bppp/p1nqp3/3n3b/3P4/NPP2N1P/2B.text:
The queenside is where we are the strongest, so we will continue playing there and prepare ...b5.

White might play Nc4 and Nce5 here, when we can trade on e5.

We may have to defend our kingside by returning our knight to f6.

r4rk1/pp2bppp/1nnqp3/7b/3P4/NPP2N1P/2B2P.text:
What I mean is, that after d4...

We can centralize the knight and target the weak c3-pawn.

White pushed both b- and d-pawns and the c3-pawn was left behind in the process.

Now pushing it to c4 would only weaken White's position further.

r4rk1/pp2bppp/2nqp3/3n3b/3P4/NPP2N1P/2BB.text: Instead, White has to resort to protecting it passively.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n1q4/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBP1.text:
White activates the knight, and it's important to know our plans here.

We want to push ...e5 and ...f6 and play on the dark squares to solidify our center.

However, it might be uncomfortable to do so with our queen on d6, so let's trade the queens. We'll give a check on e6.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n1q4/8/2pP4/2P5/PPB2PP.text:
If White goes for d4 at any point here, always capture en passant.

There is no reason to leave White's pawns on d4 and c3.

We'll capture and get rid of their d-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n1q4/8/8/2PQ4/PPB2PPP/.text:
A queen trade is fine.

Because it gives us more space to maneuver.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1n2q3/8/2p5/2P2N2/PPBPQ.text:
White blocks.

The exchange is fine for us because White will lose castling rights.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/1n6/4p3/8/2PB4/PP3PPP/RN.text:
And we'll expand in the center, with the knight coming to c6.

The other pieces will join the game soon. ...f6, Be6 and Be7. 

White hasn't accomplished anything playing like this.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1n6/2p1P3/8/1BP5/PP1P1.text:
Which retreats to b3.

Now we can push ...c4 and attack it further.

This is convenient because it prevents d4 as well.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/1n6/4P3/2p5/2P5/PPBP1P.text:
The bishop has to retreat to c2.

We got what we wanted and now White's pawn on e5 is misplaced.

White won't be connecting the pawns.

We'll push ...d6 and undermine it.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p1P3/8/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
White pushes, attacking our knight.

We'll jump into the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/2B5/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
4.Bc4 is played 8% of the time, and it certainly looks odd.

White attacks our knight but willingly gives us time and momentum to expand.

We'll begin by counter-attacking the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/2P2N2/PP1P1P.text:
Although it's only played 11% of the time, 4.Nf3 is the second most popular move.

It's played in more than 180,000 games.

White develops first and delays pushing the d-pawn.

We'll make a flexible move too and develop our knight to c6.

Now after d4 cxd4 the position would transpose to known territory.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n1P4/8/2p5/2P5/PPBP1PP.text:
White captures on d6.

Not much else to do.

We'll recapture with the queen and keep our pawns together.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.text:
The Alapin.

We'll develop the knight and attack the e-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
We are still examining the Alapin, but let's consider some sidelines in this study - namely 4.Nf3 and 4.Bc4.

White might want to surprise us and go for development before pushing in the center.

We'll learn how to counter this by sometimes even pushing our pawn to c4 and preventing d4 from coming with full effect.

White begins with e4. We'll reply with the Sicilian.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/5P2/5N2/PPPP2.text:
White develops their knight.

Now we develop our light-squared bishop to g4, pinning the f3-knight.

If White ever decides to challenge our bishop, we can simply respond by capturing White's knight.

r2qkb1r/pp3p1p/2n1bnp1/2p5/2P2P2/2N2N2/P.text:
And we prepare to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop with ...g6.

We've got more than sufficient compensation for the pawn. Our lead in development is clear and White's extra d-pawn isn't felt.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2ppP3/5Pb1/5N2/PPP.text:
And we develop our knight out to the edge, eyeing the f5-square.

We're doing well here and can look to proceed with ...Nf5 and ...Be7.

Kingside castling is also on the cards, but we don't need to rush.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2ppP3/5Pb1/5N2/PPPPB.text:
White plays Be2, breaking the pin and preparing kingside castling.

We go ...e6, opening up our other bishop and supporting the center.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/4bn2/2p5/2P2P2/5N2/PP1P2.text:
White develops their g1-knight, supporting a d-pawn advance.

We'll develop our queenside knight in order to control the d4-square.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pP4/2P2P2/8/PP1P2P.text:
The only way for White to hold onto the pawn is to support it with c4.

But now we can go ...e6 and challenge White's structure!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4Pn2/2p5/2P2P2/8/PP1P2PP.text:
White captures the e-pawn.

And we recapture with our bishop.

We're down a pawn, but have a significant lead in development.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.text:
And as early as move two, White decides to advance their f-pawn. This happens about 5% of the time,  which accounts for more than 28 million games. 

White's idea is to take space and control more of the center.

This pawn push resembles the Grand Prix Attack, but a crucial downside for White is that there's no piece controlling the d5-square.

Against this, we'll strike in the center with our d-pawn and challenge White's structure.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pP4/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.text:
White's other option is to take.

Against this, it's important that we don't recapture with our queen.

Instead, we'll develop our kingside knight and try to recapture with it. 

This is known as the Tal Gambit, since it gives White the option to try and hold onto the extra pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2ppP3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/R.text:
Half the time, White closes the center by advancing their e-pawn.

I suggest that we proceed by developing our queenside knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This chapter will deal with some of White's other, more random and uncommon options on move two.

These options aren't the best for White, but it's still important for us to know how to deal with them.

White begins with 1.e4, and we'll respond with the Sicilian.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/1qn5/3pP3/1p1P4/P4N2/2P.text: White develops their kingside knight and defends the d-pawn.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP1N2.text:
White develops their other knight.

Now we'll play ...d6, supporting c5 and controlling the e5-square.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2np2p1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP1N2.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop and prepares castling.

Now we'll advance ...e6, controlling the d5-square and preparing to develop our other knight to e7.

r1bqk2r/pp2npbp/2npp1p1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP1N2.text:
And we develop our other knight.

Our position is great. The dark-squared bishop is a beast and White's position is cramped without much forward mobility.

Our plan here is to castle and plant the c6-knight onto the d4-square.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/2B1P3/2P2Q2/.text:
And now we advance our d-pawn!

With the big center and excellent development, we're clearly better.

Our plan will be to develop the dark-squared bishop and castle.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP4/P.text:
White plays d3, supporting c4 and e4, and opening up the c1-bishop.

We'll proceed by fianchettoing.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P.text:
White also develops their knight.

And now I suggest we go for ...g6, preparing to fianchetto our bishop.

Since White has commited their c-pawn, our bishop will be powerful along the dark-squared diagonal.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/1p1P4/8/P1P2PP.text:
Against this, we can simply develop our queenside knight.

We are up a pawn and White doesn't have adequate compensation.

We'll develop our light-squared bishop and follow up with ...e6.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3pP3/1p1P4/P7/2P2PP.text:
White supports the e5-pawn.

Now we'll bring our queen out with an attack on White's d4-pawn.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/1qn5/3pP3/1p1P2b1/P4N2/2P.text:
And we develop our light-squared bishop to g4, pinning the f3-knight.

Black is better here. We are up a pawn, have great development and White's center is pretty unstable.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/3q4/1b6/5N2/2PP1PPP/.text:
And we recapture with our bishop.

We're up a pawn and White doesn't have sufficient compensation.

We'll proceed by developing our kingside knight and castling.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/3q4/3P4/5N2/P4PPP/R.text:
And we prepare to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop with ...g6.

We're just up a clean pawn here.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/3q4/1p6/P4N2/2PP1PPP/.text:
White now develops their kingside knight, defending against ...Qe5+.

We should proceed with ...e6 to open up our dark-squared bishop.

rnb1kbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3q4/1p6/P4N2/2PP1PPP.text: We should proceed with ...e6 to open up our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2p5/2B1P3/5Q2/PPP.text:
White moves their queen to safety.

We'll develop our other knight.

Our intention is to jump the knight to d4, from where it will pressure c2 and enable ...b5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3P4/1pPP4/8/P4PPP/R.text:
White advances their c-pawn in order to protect the pawn on d5.

But now we can take en passant!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3P4/3P4/2N5/P4PPP/R.text:
White recaptures with their knight.

Now we'll capture the d5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/3N4/3P4/8/P4PPP/R1BQK.text:
White decides to trade the knights.

We'll recapture with our queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p4Q/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
White usually proceeds by developing their bishop.

Now we'll exploit White's misplaced queen by developing our knight with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p4Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
White can also bring their queen out and attack the c5-pawn.

Their idea is to develop the light-squared bishop to c4 and quickly put pressure against the f7-pawn.

This, however, isn't very good.

We'll respond by opening up our bishop and defending the c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/1P2P3/8/P1PP1PPP.text:
White can also push their b-pawn.

This is called the "Wing Gambit". White goes for this merely 1% of the games, with the idea to deflect our c-pawn away to gain control over the d4-square.

The gambit isn't great, but we do need to know how to deal with it.

We'll respond by taking the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
White pushes their c-pawn, taking  space and clamping down on d5.

This is the most common of the three moves that interest us and will lead to a more closed game.

We'll develop our queenside knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1p1PP3/8/P1P2PPP/R.text:
White can also immediately take the center with their d-pawn.

This is played 31% of the time.

We'll respond by counterattacking in the center with our d-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/R.text:
White often proceeds by challenging the b-pawn with a3, called the Marshall Variation.

This is played 57% of the time.

The idea behind this is that if we now take the a-pawn, they get to develop their dark-squared bishop.

The best way to deal with a3 is to strike in the center with ...d5!

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3P4/1p1P4/8/P1P2PPP/R.text:
White can also take the d-pawn.

It's important that we don't recapture with our queen.

Instead, we should play ...Nf6 in order to recapture with our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3P4/1p6/P7/2PP1PPP/RN.text:
White can also take the pawn.

We'll recapture with the queen.

This recapture comes with a devastating threat of ...Qe5+ to fork the white king and a1-rook.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/1p1P4/8/P1P2PPP/.text: More often, White advances their e-pawn, keeping the center closed.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3pP3/1p6/P7/2PP1PPP/R.text:
More often, White advances their e-pawn, keeping the center closed.

We'll respond by developing our knight and attacking the e-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
We're continuing our analysis of White's random second moves.

This study will deal with three other moves of interest: 2.b4, 2.c4 and the early queen attack with 2.Qh5.

White opens with the king's pawn.

We'll respond with ...c5, the Sicilian.

1rbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2nppnp1/2p5/4PP2/P1NP4/B.text:
In response to White's kingside aggression, we'll play on the queenside!

We are going for ...a6 and ...b5, followed by ...b4.

A sharp battle is about to commence.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npb1/2n3pp/2pp4/7B/P1NP4/BPP.text:
White tries to keep the pin...

But not for long, as we'll break it with g5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npb1/2n4p/2pp2p1/8/P1NP2B1/B.text: The bishop finally slides to g3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2n3p1/2pp2B1/8/P1NP4/BP.text:
An option is certainly 6.Bg5, pinning our knight.

White is threatening to capture on d5.

So we should do something about the bishop right away.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2nppnp1/2p5/4PP2/P1NP4/B.text:
White does indeed grab space with the f-pawn.

But e5 is covered.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2B1P3/P1NP.text:
One of the options is Nf3, but it doesn't do much about our plan.

This move is played 18% of the time.

We'll still try to prepare ...d5 with our knight.

The most popular move in this position is Nge2, played almost a third of the time.

White doesn't commit their knight to f3 but rather develops it to the safe e2-square.

Also, there could be f4 lurking at some point.

We'll continue with our standard ideas, and prepare ...d5.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/4P3/P1NP4/.text:
White preemptively retreats with the bishop and discourages ...d5, because it doesn't come with tempo.

Now going for ...d6 is just fine.

Instead of the setup with the knight on e7, we'll put our knight on f6 and remain solid.

Then we'll look to play on the queenside.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2B1P3/P1NP4/.text:
So, White connects the pawns.

And we'll play on the light squares, too.

Let's see how White can approach the game now.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2npp1p1/2p5/4P3/P1NP4/BP.text:
White activates the knight to e2, because they might want to move the f-pawn in the near future.

We'll continue natural development in this line and play Nf6.

There are many nuances in every opening, and this is one of them.

Knowing how to adapt to your opponent's play is crucial.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpb1/2n1p1pp/2p5/2B1P2B/P1NP.text:
White retreats to h4.

And we'll continue chasing it with ...g5.

This is all so that we can get our central expansion underway.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpb1/2n1p2p/2p3p1/2B1P3/P1NP.text:
The bishop escapes to g3.

And we can finally play ...d5.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpbp/2n1p1p1/2p3B1/2B1P3/P1N.text:
White can pin it our knight, but that gives us momentum.

Don't be afraid to extend a lot here.

We can attack the bishop with h6 first.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2B1P3/P1NP4.text:
White castles...

And we can push in the center immediately.

r1bqk2r/pp2n1b1/2n4p/2pp1pp1/8/P1NP1NB1/.text:
We've got ...f5 to continue the aggression!

We'll play ...f4 even if White goes for h3.

Their bishops will be completely restricted, while we'll have gotten the space we need.

We'll castle as well and place the bishop on e6 from where it covers the d5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2npb1/2n1p2p/2pP2p1/2B5/P1NP1N.text:
