Capturing on d5 is a big mistake.

We'll keep the attack on the bishop and open up our own.

r1bqk2r/pp2npb1/2n4p/2pp2p1/8/P1NP1NB1/B.text:
White retreats to a2.

How to further harass White?

r1bqk2r/pp2npbp/2n1p1p1/2pP4/2B5/P1NP4/1.text:
White takes once.

We'll recapture and keep our center together.

Our light-squared bishop is now open, too.

r1bqk2r/pp2npbp/2n3p1/2pp4/8/P1NP4/BPP1N.text:
White retreats to a2 and keeps their bishop safe.

We got what we wanted in the center.

So it's time to castle and await White's next move.

r1bqk2r/pp3pbp/2nppnp1/2p5/4P3/P1NP4/BPP.text:
White castles...

And so will we.

r2q1rk1/pp2npb1/2n1b2p/2pp2p1/8/P1NP2B1/.text:
And we'll reinforce our center with ...Be6.

Our kingside is safe because the bishop on g7 defends. We control the center, which is why we're better.

There are some light-squared weaknesses but White's bishop is nowhere near our king.

If White goes for f4, ...d4 is a strong response.

Otherwise, we could improve our knight with ...Nf5.

rn3rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pq1b2/1P6/P1P2N2/3P.text:
The f5-square is most active for the bishop.

Now that we've developed all the pieces, d4 isn't as potent, but it will probably come.

In that case, capturing on d4 and playing ...Nc6 is a good idea.

If this happens, we can also play ...a5 down the line.

rnb1k1nr/pp2ppbp/6p1/2pq4/1P6/P1P2N2/3P1.text:
White activates the knight now.

And we'll do the same, preparing castling.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pq4/1P6/P1P2N2/3PB.text:
Sort of admitting defeat and giving up on any central play, White continues kingside development.

We'll castle.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pq4/1P6/P1P2N2/3PB.text:
And so will White.

It's time to finish our development as well.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1Np1/2p5/1P2P3/P7/1BP.text:
White takes on f6, which is the most natural.

And here's an important move to remember.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3p1pp1/2p5/1P2P3/P7/1BPP.text:
We'll recapture with the pawn!

White's kingside pieces aren't out yet and they are far away from castling.

We can take advantage of that by opening up the e-file and going for ...Re8 and ...f5!

Our knight is coming to c6 as well and we've already got a slight advantage.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/1P2P3/P1N5/2PP.text:
Blocking with the knight is playable.

Let's form a pawn chain with d6.

If White takes on c5, we'll just recapture and keep a pawn there.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/1P2P3/P1P5/3P1.text:
White blocks the diagonal with the c-pawn.

They create a dark-squared pawn chain and are now threatening to capture on c5.

But we won't defend the pawn. We'll strike in the center instead!

Active approaches in the center like this are often a good idea against flank advances in the opening.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/2B1P3/P1N5/1PP.text:
White goes ahead and activates the bishop as well.

Both sides will develop in the next few moves.

We'll get the knight out to c6.

When the bishop is on c4 (and White didn't have many better squares for it) I suggest we go for ...e6 and ...d5 at some point.

We saw this motif in the previous chapters of the course.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2p5/1P2P3/P1N5/1B.text:
They fianchetto instead.

But now our knight comes to f6, and there's already a threat in the position.

We are threatening to capture on e4 and exploit the pin on White's knight on c3.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/6p1/2pP4/1P6/P1P5/3P1PP.text:
White captures on d5.

And now our queen defends the c-pawn.

And there is no Nc3 since White already played c3, which is one of the reasons we played ...d5 in this line in the first place.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pN4/1P2P3/P7/1BP.text:
White jumps to d5 instead and tries to exploit the pin themselves!

We won't bite, of course.

Let's castle instead and keep our bishop protected.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/1P2P3/P7/2PP1P.text:
The most common move in this position is b4 anyway, and it's played 45% of the time.

But it's not the best move in the long run.

We'll develop and attack the rook, which is what we wanted.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/4P3/P1N5/1PPP1.text:
White doesn't have to rush with b4 and can instead opt for development here, and they do so 13% of the time.

But now it's like a Closed Sicilian where we got an extra tempo because White played the dubious a3. Of course, this favours us!

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP/.text:
Already on move 2, White plays a3.

It's played less than 1% of the time, but there are still almost 3 million games played from this position in the database.

White simply wants b4 to undermine our c5-pawn in order to later play in the center.

The bishop often comes to b2.

We'll anticipate White's plans and play ...g6. We want to be quicker with play on the long diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This chapter will take a look at the rarest of the sidelines: 2.a3 and 2.b3.

In particular, this study will deal with 2.a3 where White tries to go for the quick b4 and Bb2.

Of course, these setups are not optimal for White as they disregard the center in the first few moves, but they may come as a surprise if we're not sure about our lines.

Let's begin with 1.e4 c5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/2p5/4P3/1PNP1N2.text:
And we'll castle.

Our bishop has contested the diagonal, and we'll complement our central play on the light squares with pawn moves like ...e6 and ...d5.

A great position for Black.

r1bqkb1r/pp1np2p/2n2pp1/2p5/2P5/PP6/1B1P.text:
We'll recapture with the knight this time so that we have a developing square for it. It can reroute to b6.

Our bishop is coming to either g7 or h6 and we'll castle.

If White plays Nf3, we can pin that knight with ...Bg4 at some point.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/2p5/4P3/1PN2N2/.text:
Both knights are now out for White.

We'll complete the fianchetto, and there is the threat of ...Nxe4 lurking.

White's knight is potentially pinned to the bishop.

rnb1kb1r/pp1qp2p/5pp1/2pn4/8/1P6/PBPP1PP.text:
We'll recapture with the queen, because we want our knight on c6 and our bishop fianchettoed on b7.

In this line, our dark-squared bishop will have a much better time on h6 than on g7, since there's a pawn on f6.

A good improving square for our knight in the center is the f4-square.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p1P3/1n6/NP3Q2/PBP.text:
We'll use the time to play ...Bg7.

Now e6 isn't scary because we can castle, which we are planning to do anyway.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p1P3/8/1PB5/P1PP1P.text:
And we'll fianchetto, contesting the diagonal.

Suddenly, the e5-pawn can become a target after ...Nc6.

A good idea would be either ...d6 or ...d5, as well.

Remember, if White pushes e6 now, simply castle and you're fine.

rnbqkb1r/pp1Pp2p/5pp1/2pn4/8/1P6/PBPP1PP.text: White has to resort to capturing on d7 instead.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2n1P1p1/2p5/2P5/PP6/1B.text:
You will probably see e6 as White doesn't want to give us easy development.

As in the main line, ...f6 solves our problems.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/4P1p1/2pn4/8/1P6/PBPP1.text:
5.e6 is played 61% of the time, but isn't the best for White.

Sure, the bishop is eyeing our rook and there is a pawn on the sixth rank.

But there's no need to panic.

We'll prevent exf7+ and save the rook by blocking the diagonal with f6.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2p1P3/8/1P6/PBPP1.text:
White will most likely push the pawn to e5, and they do so 55% of the time.

The idea is to remove our knight from the diagonal and then reintroduce the threat to our rook.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2p5/4P3/1PN5/PBPP.text:
White can go the calmer route here and simply develop.

This move is played 10% of the time.

We'll do the same, playing Nc6.

The game doesn't have to be full of fireworks for us to get a good position.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p1P3/1n6/NP3Q2/PB.text:
White defends with Na3.

But our last move was important because it gave us a tempo.

If White had tried 6.e6, then f6 would keep everything defended and it's slightly better for Black.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p1P3/1nP5/PP6/1B1.text:
This provokes White to push another pawn.

Our knight has had quite a journey, but it's landed on c6 where it's safe.

We are planning to finally fianchetto.

Let's see how White can proceed now.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pnP3/2P5/1P6/PB1P.text:
A move that's played almost 20% of the time is c4.

Again, it's not one of the best moves because it's simply a crude attack on our knight.

White doesn't benefit from this one-move threat in the long run.

We'll just slide to b4.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pnP3/8/1P3Q2/PBPP.text:
A peculiar-looking move is certainly 5.Qf3, although it's not a mistake.

White attacks our knight without committing another pawn forward.

Also, the queen is hitting the f7-pawn and e6 is the plan at some point.

We'll jump to b4 and threaten a fork on c2, since the queen has left the d1-post.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pnP3/8/1P6/PBPP1P.text:
We'll move to the center.

White has a lot of options here.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pnP3/8/1PN5/PBPP1.text:
The best move in the position is probably 5.Nc3.

White doesn't push e6 or c4 prematurely but rather offers a trade of knights and wants a positional game.

We'll accept.

There's not much merit in retreating.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2p5/4P3/1P6/PBPP1P.text:
White can get there first.

But we'll block the diagonal with the knight.

This is where things could get "tricky".

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.text:
2.b3 is played less than 1% of the time, but that's still in more than 2.7 million games.

As mentioned, White wants to fianchetto the bishop and keep it active on the long diagonal, covering the d4-square.

This is a sound plan if we don't do anything about it.

But we will fight on the diagonal!

Our bishop is coming to g7, too.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will show 2.b3 in the Sicilian, which aims to quickly fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and pose problems on the long diagonal.

Some of the lines here might look scary, but they aren't if we know what we're dealing with.

Let's begin with 1.e4. We'll reply with the SIcilian.
